title: Dorsal and Ventral Attention Networks

html:
The brain’s attentional machinery splits into two tightly coupled, largely supramodal systems 1. A dorsal fronto-parietal network (DAN) implements sustained, goal-directed selection and sampling; a ventral fronto-temporo-parietal network (VAN) acts as a right-lateralized interrupt/reorienting system that detects behaviorally relevant changes and rapidly resets the dorsal controller. This division is supported by converging lesion, neurophysiology, and imaging results: damage to right ventral frontoparietal cortex (including TPJ/IFG) yields classic spatial neglect 2 and broader deficits in reorienting and vigilance 3, while dorsal lesions impair voluntary orienting and priority mapping. Functionally, DAN supplies the "spotlight operator" that amplifies task-relevant channels, and VAN detects behaviorally relevant violations of expectation and rapidly resets DAN’s priorities to reorient sampling 1. Average effective connectivity across task conditions (Figure) 48. Task conditions modulate network effective connectivity (Figure).

DAN is anchored in intraparietal sulcus/superior parietal lobule (IPS/SPL) and in frontal eye field / superior precentral sulcus (FEF/sPCS).

The intraparietal sulcus (IPS) is anatomically a crossroads and functionally a Swiss army knife-exactly what you want for building and maintaining a supramodal priority map. Its subdivisions tile distinct effector and sensory interfaces: LIP encodes gaze-centered spatial priority for saccades 4; MIP/PRR (PRR = "parietal reach region") codes reach targets 5, 6; VIP integrates vision with tactile and vestibular signals to represent peripersonal space 7; and AIP specifies object shape, orientation, and grip postures for hand use and tools 8. This mosaic lets IPS fuse "where" with "how" across effectors and modalities and project that synthesis to downstream controllers. The same territory also carries abstract magnitudes-hIPS responds to amodal numerosity and quantity 9-illustrating how IPS sits high enough in the hierarchy to host amodal control variables yet remains topographically organized for spatial selection. This blend of multisensory convergence, effector specificity, and topographic coding is what makes IPS the natural substrate for a manipulable, task-coupled priority map 10, 11.

Frontal eye field (FEF; in humans centered around the superior precentral sulcus, sPCS) is wired to read out the parietal map into sampling policies and to write precise, retinotopically aligned gain commands back into sensory cortex. Subthreshold microstimulation at a given FEF locus boosts V4 responses at the corresponding visual-field location and reproduces classic signatures of voluntary attention 12, 13; concurrent TMS-fMRI in humans shows the same causal direction of influence from FEF/sPCS to early visual cortices with perceptual consequences 14. Anatomically, FEF has privileged two-way lines to the superior colliculus and receives a corollary-discharge loop via mediodorsal thalamus, giving it online access to where the eyes are going next and enabling predictive updates ("remapping") of attention pointers so perception stays stable across saccades 15. Functionally, this means FEF can schedule the next fixation, pre-amplify the corresponding sensory channels, and confirm execution through subcortical loops-tight, millisecond-scale control that a pure parietal node lacks on its own.

Long-range white-matter scaffolding explains why these nodes act as a single controller even when they compute different pieces of the problem. The dorsal branches of the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF I/II) link IPS to dorsal frontal cortex (including FEF/sPCS), supporting fast bidirectional exchange between map maintenance and readout modules; where these tracts are compromised, voluntary orienting suffers and neglect risk rises, matching the clinical asymmetries seen after right-hemisphere lesions 16. Retinotopic mapping confirms the architectural logic: IPS and sPCS contain attention-driven visual-field maps whose coupling to V1 varies with the locus of attention 17, 18, consistent with a controller that dynamically "opens" communication channels to the currently prioritized sector of sensory cortex. A diffusion-MRI atlas maps the superior longitudinal fasciculus (Figure) 49. A published diagram identifies the two attention networks (Figure) 51.

Putting it together: IPS maintains the continuously computed, multisensory priority landscape and translates it into effector-specific coordinates (eyes, hands, body), while FEF turns the current peak into a timed sampling policy and precision-gated sensory gain-backed by subcortical loops for rapid execution and corollary discharge for predictive stability. This division of labor is why DAN can both "think ahead" (goal-biased maps in IPS) and "act now" (FEF-driven gain and saccade scheduling) with latencies compatible with real-world behavior like reading a road sign at speed, catching a tossed object, or switching from a wrench to pliers mid-repair.

VAN’s core lies in right temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and ventral/lateral prefrontal cortex (often IFG/MFG).

TPJ is a heteromodal convergence zone bordering posterior STS and inferior parietal lobule, perched near the transmodal apex of cortex along the principal gradient from sensory to abstract processing 19, 20. That location and its broad connectivity to control and default-mode systems make TPJ ideal for computing model-level surprise: integrating context, expectations, and multisensory evidence to decide when ongoing sampling should be interrupted. White-matter anatomy explains the rapid TPJ-to-PFC handshake: the ventral branch of the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF III) links inferior parietal (TPJ) to ventral frontal cortex (IFG) 21, and exhibits strong rightward lateralization that tracks individual differences in spatial attention bias and neglect risk.

IFG/MFG translate detection into enforcement. Right IFG has a hyperdirect projection to subthalamic nucleus (STN), giving VAN a monosynaptic brake on basal-ganglia output that can halt ongoing motor and cognitive programs while priorities are recomputed 22, 23. MFG sits at the handshake with the dorsal attention network (DAN): it routes the interrupt so DAN can retarget the priority map, and-during sustained focus-helps DAN suppress VAN’s chatter. Thalamic partners (especially pulvinar) provide timing that opens and closes communication windows between sensory and control cortices, and LC-norepinephrine bursts supply the state switch that makes the reset global.

Net effect: while you’re locked on a phone number, a siren or your name from behind spikes TPJ, IFG slams the brake via STN, MFG hands the new locus to DAN, and pulvinar/LC orchestrate the system-wide flip-typically within a couple hundred milliseconds.

DAN’s top-down control is largely carried on slow alpha-beta rhythms that bias cortical excitability and open phase-aligned "communication windows" for fast, feedforward gamma activity; when a salient event engages VAN, it triggers a rapid phase reset of these slow rhythms so the windows reopen at the new locus 24, 25, 26, 27. The pulvinar functions as the timing switchboard for this exchange: during selection it synchronizes and phase-aligns nodes such as FEF, LIP, and V4/TEO-predominantly in theta/alpha-low-beta bands-to route information among the right cortical partners at the right moments 28, 29. In humans and macaques, feedback-like influences preferentially ride alpha-beta while feedforward signals ride gamma, providing a frequency-multiplexed channel structure that the pulvinar can gate 30. By modulating interareal coherence (rather than only mean firing rates), this thalamic brokerage enables swift, low-latency handoffs between goal-directed (DAN) and stimulus-driven (VAN) modes and couples top-down setpoints to bottom-up sensory flow in a behaviorally advantageous way 31.

Beneath the cortical controller sits a fast, phylogenetically old subcortical layer that both seeds and shapes what DAN and VAN will deal with in the first place. The superior colliculus (SC) is a stacked sensorimotor map: superficial layers receive direct retinal and early cortical input; intermediate/deep layers integrate visual, auditory, and somatosensory cues with motor commands for gaze, head, and body turns. In primates, SC neurons signal salient onsets within  50 ms and even show short-latency category preferences (e.g., faces) 32, giving the system an ultra-rapid, coarse priority sketch that can bias covert selection before cortex has finished its recurrent work. Causally, inactivating SC degrades covert attention and the selection of task-informative signals without requiring eye movements 33, while dorsal fronto-parietal outputs pre-tune SC: FEF/sPCS can sharpen or damp SC visual bursts on a tens-of-milliseconds timescale, aligning subcortical orienting with current goals 34. Through the inferior/mediodorsal pulvinar, SC routes these "first pass" salience estimates to extrastriate cortex and to the amygdala, forming a quick subcortical conduit that can flag biologically urgent events even when V1 pathways are compromised 35. An October 2026 experiment tests thalamic involvement in attention (Figure) 50. The experiment measures visuospatial performance (Figure).

Zooming in on the amygdala clarifies why an "ancient" structure is still indispensable to human attention control. The basolateral complex (BLA) sits at a convergence of fast, coarse subcortical input and rich, high-level cortical descriptions: in primates it receives a rapid magnocellular-biased stream routed via superior colliculus -> pulvinar (a pathway that is present anatomically and functionally in humans) 36, 37 while also ingesting detailed ventral-stream signals from inferotemporal/perirhinal cortex 38. Within  74 ms of a threat-like image, human intracranial recordings show the amygdala firing before visual cortex, consistent with that subcortical route and low-spatial-frequency sensitivity 39. From this hub, the BLA sends feedback to visual cortex-including V1 and TE-via synapse-forming, layer-targeted projections that up-weight behaviorally important features 40; lesion/inactivation work in humans and macaques shows that without the amygdala, the usual "emotional boost" of extrastriate responses disappears and perceptual sensitivity to biologically relevant cues is blunted 41. Computationally, single-unit studies reveal neurons that multiplex value with space 42, 43, tracking which location is currently worth sampling and biasing gaze toward reward-predictive or ethologically salient stimuli; when the amygdala is silenced, value/context-driven facilitation of saccades is diminished, an effect that can be mediated by amygdalo-nigral access to basal ganglia output channels controlling eye movements 44. The amygdala also has privileged levers on global state: it can recruit basal forebrain cholinergic 45 and locus-coeruleus noradrenergic systems, producing arousal-biased competition that selectively amplifies high-priority representations (and, via NE "hotspots," potently suppresses distractors 46), thus handing VAN a system-wide reset while boosting DAN’s gain at the newly prioritized locus. Finally, its coupling to posterior STS/TPJ and ventral/lateral prefrontal territories links social/affective relevance to reorienting control, with task-dependent amygdala-rTPJ connectivity changes in humans underscoring this ventral network handshake 47. In short, the amygdala’s unique combination of speed, associative plasticity, bidirectional sensory links, and direct access to arousal and oculomotor gates makes it the brain’s affect-weighted "priority injector" into DAN/VAN rather than a redundant relic.
